quiz2.q: Which of these prompts is most likely to trigger a hallucination?
options: "Draft a five-section outline for a real estate market report"
"Explain in simple terms how a mortgage works"
"Give the exact date and decree number of the ministry's little-known 2011 reform"
"Rewrite this letter in a friendlier tone"
quiz2.explain: The more specific and rare the fact, the more blurrily it's stored in the weights — and the model will confidently reconstruct a plausible invention. General explanations, outlines, and reworking text pasted into the chat all rest on reliably compressed patterns.

quiz2.q: A friend insists: "ChatGPT remembered I'm a vegetarian — so the model must be learning from our conversations." What's actually going on?
options: The service stores notes about the user in an ordinary database and slips them into the start of every dialogue — the model's weights themselves are frozen
The model retrains on users' conversations every night, and its weights gradually change
Inside the neural network there's a dedicated long-term memory module where facts about the person are recorded
The model recognizes the user by their writing style and reconstructs facts about them from general patterns
quiz2.explain: The model doesn't learn from conversations: the weights have been fixed since training. The "memory" is a service add-on: the notes live in an external database and are quietly inserted into the context window of each new chat.

quiz2.q: You write to the model: "Look over my lease agreement and find the risky clauses" — but you never pasted the agreement's text into the chat. What's the most likely unpleasant outcome?
options: The model will find the agreement on the internet through indirect clues and analyze it
The model will hang: without the file it physically has nothing to process
No harm done: models always honestly report that they can't see the document
The model may confidently produce a plausible "analysis" of an agreement it has never seen
quiz2.explain: The model sees only what made it into the context window, and it was trained to continue text plausibly — in its training data, a request for an analysis is usually followed by an analysis. Sometimes it will honestly ask for the text, but you can't count on that: paste the document into the chat yourself.

quiz2.q: You pasted a 400-page report into the chat (it still fits in the context window) and are asking questions about the details. Which details is the model most likely to miss?
options: From the beginning of the report — it gets cut from the context window first
From the middle — attention is worse at finding details in the middle of a long text than at its beginning and end
None: as long as the text fits in the window, all its parts are processed equally accurately
From the end — toward the end of a long text the model "tires" and reads less attentively
quiz2.explain: A long context isn't free: the attention mechanism is worse at fishing details out of the middle of a large text, which is why important passages should sit close to the question. Trimming the beginning happens only when the dialogue stops fitting in the window.

quiz2.q: For which task is it reasonable to switch on deep reasoning mode, despite the cost in time and tokens?
options: Asking what year Saint Petersburg was founded
Rewriting a paragraph of a letter in a formal tone
Building a duty roster for six employees with a dozen overlapping constraints
Asking for a list of synonyms for the word "important"
quiz2.explain: A reasoning draft helps where the answer takes many steps and self-checking: each written step becomes a foothold for the next. For simple questions it's "taking a tank to buy bread" — overpaying in time and tokens with no gain in quality.

quiz2.q: Why does the advice "break a complex task into steps: first an outline, then section by section" genuinely improve the result?
options: Every intermediate result lands in the context and serves as a foothold for the next predictions — the same principle as reasoning models
Between your messages, the model gets extra time to mull the task over
Short prompts burn fewer tokens, and in economy mode the model answers more accurately
With every new message the model retrains a little on your task
quiz2.explain: The model predicts a continuation of whatever sits in the context: the finished outline and written sections become the footing for the next step. Between requests it ponders nothing and learns nothing — only the text in the window does the work.

exercises.q: Explain in your own words why it's wrong to say "the model lied" about a hallucination — and why it's not a glitch that can simply be fixed.
exercises.ref: Lying presupposes knowing the truth and hiding it, but the model has no store of facts to check against — only weights holding the patterns of texts. It always does one and the same thing: reconstructs the most plausible continuation. For frequent facts, the plausible coincides with the true; in place of a rare, blurrily stored fact, it just as confidently reconstructs an invention. That's the flip side of the very principle of text prediction, not a separate malfunction.

exercises.q: Predict what happens: yesterday you spent two hours discussing a book outline with the model, and today you opened a new chat and wrote "Let's continue with chapter three." The service's "memory" feature is switched off. How will the model behave, and what should you have done instead?
exercises.ref: A new chat is a blank slate: the same frozen weights and an empty context window — yesterday's conversation doesn't exist for the model. It will either ask which book you mean, or — more insidiously — confidently press on with some plausible "chapter three" you never discussed. The right move is to start the new chat with a brief recap of yesterday's conclusions: the model receives context only through the window.

exercises.q: Come up with your own example of two prompts: one where the answer can be trusted almost without checking, and another where verification against a primary source is mandatory. Explain the difference through how the model works.
exercises.ref: For example: "explain the difference between leasing and renting" — versus "what's the government fee for registering a lease in 2026." General explanations rest on patterns repeated thousands of times in the training texts and reliably compressed into the weights. A specific rare fact — a figure, a date, a number, a quote — is stored blurrily, and the model will confidently reconstruct a plausible value. The rule: the more specific and rare the fact, and the higher the cost of an error, the more mandatory the check.
